summary: Eight shallow spots. The synthesizer's three self-flagged sections all confirmed weak (Source Tensions, Verdict, MoE & EP) and each gets a finding. Beyond them: the DDP overhead derivation does not reproduce its own headline (units flip GiB/GB; 6.6% vs the table's 7.1%) and silently assumes bf16 gradient buckets that AMP does not provide; the Engram section stops at the byte count and never gives the retrieval mechanism; the CSA2 section lists five stacks but never gives the wgmma/mma.sync or 8%-of-peak mechanism that makes the port hard; and the frozen-table design is 11x internally inconsistent in the repo's own docs (33M entries/layer implies 135 GB/layer) while sitting at rho=0 on Engram's published allocation law. No interim note is wholly ignored; all six are cited below.
most_damaging: depth-1 -- the frozen-table memory budget resolves an 11x internal inconsistency in the repo silently. If research.md SS3's '33M entries per grafted layer' is what the repo means, the table is 135 GB/layer and 270 GB for two layers, and the query's third claim ('frozen tables make 7B/1B fit DDP on 64 GB') is false rather than 'True at ~43.1 GB'. The report's 'True' verdict rests on adopting the paper's 3M entries/layer without saying so.

findings.location: ## Engram & Frozen Memory -> ### The table is 24 GB, not 12 GB. Anchor quote: "yielding 3M entries per grafted layer"
findings.issue: The report corrects the plan's SS5 frozen-table figure (6B / 12 GB total -> 12.29B / 24.58 GB) but never addresses the plan's SS3 figure, which is 11x worse and mutually inconsistent with the plan's own byte count. research.md SS3 states "33M entries per grafted layer (top 11M n-grams per order)" alongside "roughly 12 GB of frozen memory per layer". 33M x 2,048 dims x 2 B = 135.2 GB per layer; two grafted layers = 270.4 GB. If the repo means 33M entries, the frozen-table design does not fit 64 GB/card and does not fit 320 GB aggregate either. Verdict (c) returns "True, at ~43.1 GB/card" by silently adopting the paper's 3M entries/layer. That resolution is defensible, but it is unstated, so the reader cannot tell whether "True" rests on the paper's number or the plan's -- and the query's third claim turns on exactly this. Separately, the design's allocation is outside both published laws: 6B frozen of 7B total is 86% frozen, i.e. rho = 0 on Engram's allocation ratio (the fraction of the inactive-parameter budget assigned to MoE), whose optimum is rho ~ 0.75-0.80; and 86% is 1.7x LongCat's "no more than 50% of the total parameter budget to N-gram Embedding". The report never states either, so the reader cannot see that the arm sits at the boundary of the regime where the published wins were measured.
findings.evidence: interim-report-memory-budget-and-frozen-tables, section 'The frozen table is 12B params / 24.6 GB, not 6B / 12 GB -- and the repo's SS3 has an 11x transcription error': "SS3 says '33M entries per grafted layer (top 11M n-grams per order)' while keeping 'roughly 12 GB per layer' -- but 33M x 2,048 x 2 B = 135.3 GB/layer, an 11x inconsistency with its own 12 GB figure." Same note, section 'The quality premise is weaker than the repo's SS3 implies': "its allocation (86% of total parameters frozen) is far outside both published allocation laws -- Engram's U-shaped optimum ('reallocating roughly 20%-25% of the sparse parameter budget to Engram yields the best performance ... stable across regimes (rho~75%-80%)') and LongCat's 'no more than 50% of the total parameter budget to N-gram Embedding'." Primary sources: [[memory-grafting-scaling-language-model]] ("yielding 3M entries per grafted layer ... roughly 12 GB of frozen memory per layer"; Fig. 4 caption "0.92B trainable parameters with approximately 12B frozen grafting memory offloaded"); [[conditional-memory-via-scalable-lookup]] SS3.1 (allocation ratio rho in [0,1], optimum rho ~ 75-80% MoE); [[scaling-embeddings-outperforms-scaling-experts-in-language]] ("allocate no more than 50% of the total parameter budget to N-gram Embedding"). Repo: research.md lines 112-113 (33M entries vs 12 GB/layer) and line 155 (7B total, 1B trainable + 6B frozen).
findings.recommendation: In 'The table is 24 GB, not 12 GB', add the SS3 conditional explicitly: "If the repo's SS3 '33M entries per grafted layer' is what it means, the table is 135 GB/layer and 270 GB for two layers -- the design does not fit at all. The 24.58 GB figure holds only on the paper's 3M entries/layer; the repo must reconcile SS3 against SS5 before the memory budget is trusted." Then add one sentence to 'Why freeze anyway' (or a new short paragraph): the 6B/7B = 86%-frozen allocation is rho = 0 on Engram's allocation law (optimum rho ~ 0.75-0.80) and 1.7x LongCat's 50% cap, so the arm is testing the boundary of the published regime, not its optimum -- a second reason, besides the 9B budget, to expect a null. Qualify Verdict (c) with both caveats so the 'True' verdict is visibly conditional.

findings.location: ## Engram & Frozen Memory -> ### Freezing is a collective-elimination design, not a memory trick. Anchor quote: "The table costs VRAM but almost no per-token FLOPs, because a lookup is not a matmul."
findings.issue: The section gives the reader the byte count and the collective it removes, but no mechanism for how the table is actually read during training. The query asks whether frozen tables make the model fit DDP; the lookup path's fabric cost is part of 'fit', and the report never supplies it. Four pieces are missing. (a) Lookup keys depend only on input token IDs, not hidden states, so retrieval is prefetchable a layer ahead -- that is why a 100B-parameter table offloaded to host costs only 2.8% inference throughput on an H800. (b) The per-GPU lookup traffic is ~224 MB/s = ~13% of one 1.7 GB/s link at 140k tok/s aggregate (5.6% at 60k), not 80%: the repo's 1.35 GB/s figure divides aggregate-across-five-GPUs traffic by one card's bandwidth. (c) The table fits resident at 43.1 GB, so the rational choice is zero PCIe traffic; the paper's single word 'offloaded' appears once in a figure caption with no mechanism and no host/CPU mention anywhere in the text, so it does not establish that host offload is required. (d) At 32k the per-layer compute window (~1.2 s at 1B active) dwarfs lookup time, and the lookup volume (1.6 GB/GPU/step) is half the all-reduce's 3.2 GB, so the two can be scheduled apart but not overlapped without contention.
findings.evidence: interim-report-memory-budget-and-frozen-tables, section 'The offload-traffic finding does not hold at 80% -- it is ~13-16% of one link, and the table fits resident anyway': "The locus's arithmetic is 5 KB x 2 layers x 135k tok/s = 1.35 GB/s = 80% of the 1.68 GB/s link. That divides *aggregate* throughput by *one card's* bandwidth. ... per-GPU lookup traffic is 28k x 8 KB = 224 MB/s = 13% of the measured 1.7 GB/s H2D link ... At a more realistic 60k tok/s aggregate for a 1B-active model, it is 96 MB/s = 5.6%." Same note: "the lookup keys depend only on input token IDs, so retrieval can be prefetched a layer ahead -- the mechanism [[pooling-engram-conditional-memory-in-large]] describes ('Since the hash function relies on N-gram token IDs rather than intermediate hidden states, retrieval can be initiated at the start of the decoding step') and the reason [[conditional-memory-via-scalable-lookup]] measures only 2.8% inference penalty for a 100B table on H800. At 32k-token micro-batches the per-layer compute window (~1.2 s at 1B active / 162 TFLOPS per GPU) dwarfs the lookup time." Same note: "the table fits resident. The paper's 13.2B design lands at 43.1 GB with FLCE (53.1 GB naive), leaving 11-21 GB of headroom on a 64 GB card. ... There is no VRAM pressure forcing offload, so the rational choice on this box is to keep the table resident and pay zero PCIe traffic. The paper's single word 'offloaded' (in a figure caption, with no mechanism, no host/CPU mention anywhere in the text, and no measured traffic) does not establish that host offload is required." Primary sources: [[pooling-engram-conditional-memory-in-large]] ("retrieval can be initiated at the start of the decoding step"; "For an Engram module at Layer 2, the prefetch [window]"); [[conditional-memory-via-scalable-lookup]] Table 4 (100B-parameter table offload, 2.8% peak penalty, "the compute intensity of early dense blocks provides a sufficient temporal window to mask the retrieval latency"); [[tf-engram-a-train-free-engram-with-ssd-backed-memory-for]] (inference latency curve 2.108 ms/token at 1M entries -> 2.175 ms/token at 100M); [[github-dl4rcecmp-170hx-inference-lab-cmp-170hx-llm-inference-lab-vllm-scripts-me]] (H2D 1.7 GB/s at x4).
findings.recommendation: Add a short 'How the table is read' paragraph between 'Freezing is a collective-elimination design' and 'The table is 24 GB'. State: keys are token-ID-only, so retrieval is prefetchable a layer ahead; per-GPU lookup traffic is ~224 MB/s (~13% of one 1.7 GB/s link at 140k tok/s aggregate, ~5.6% at 60k) and the repo's 1.35 GB/s is aggregate-not-per-link; the table fits resident at 43.1 GB, so the design should keep it resident and pay zero PCIe traffic; and the paper's 'offloaded' is a figure-caption word with no mechanism. This converts the section from a byte count into a mechanism and closes the query's 'does it fit DDP' question on the traffic side as well as the VRAM side.

findings.location: ## Engram & Frozen Memory -> ### The measurement problem is a unit problem. Anchor quote: "So a 9B-token A/B at 500M can resolve the upper half of the expected effect range"
findings.issue: The section argues one direction only: can a 9B A/B detect the effect? It never argues the other: would a detection mean anything? Two mechanisms are missing. (a) The effect sizes it compares -- 0.0139 nats at 100B tokens and 0.082 nats at 500B tokens -- are measured at 100-500B tokens and compared against a floor measured at 3.7B tokens, with no scaling correction. The interim note's ln(tokens) projection puts the 9B deltas at ~0.0066 and ~0.029 nats: 1.7x and 7.2x the 0.004-nat floor, not the 3.5x and 20x the report claims. Engram's allocation delta is therefore marginal, not comfortably detectable, and the report's 'can resolve the upper half' overstates the margin by ~2x. (b) The dominant failure mode is ranking reversal, not the null. Tay et al. fit scaling exponents and find the dense Transformer has the steepest (alpha 0.54 upstream / 0.28 downstream) against Switch MoE (0.23/0.14) and Performer (0.25/0.05), so a 9B ranking systematically flatters every non-dense arm and can reverse at 100B; MoBA's own sweep shows its 32K penalty shrinking 2.3x (0.105 -> 0.045 nats) as compute rises; Memory Grafting's sign flips between 0.92B (-0.59 points) and 2.8B (+0.48). The report says a null would be an informative bound but never says a win would be an uninformative one -- which is the asymmetry the program actually faces.
findings.evidence: interim-report-token-budget-and-effect-size, section 'The two failure modes are opposite, and the locus has the sign backwards': "the dominant risk is different ... Ranking instability: false positive / wrong sign. This is the risk the locus missed. Tay et al. show the exponent differs and rankings flip across compute regions; MoBA shows the gap shrinks 2.3x with compute; Memory Grafting shows the memory axis's sign flips between 0.92B and 2.8B. So a 9B-token ranking of the four arms can reverse at 100B -- and the reversal is systematic, not random: the 9B point flatters non-dense architectures because the dense Transformer has the steepest exponent (alpha = 0.54 vs 0.23 for Switch, 0.25 for Performer)." Same note: "Expected deltas at 9B are ~0.007-0.04 nats (T4: scaling the 100B-token deltas down by ln(9)/ln(100) ~ 0.48), i.e. 0.25-1.5% relative -- 2-14x below the 3.5% floor. A null here is the expected result even if the effect is real and large at 100B." Primary sources: [[scaling-laws-vs-model-architectures-how-does-inductive-bias-influence-scaling]] (Table 2 alpha values; "it is difficult to get the full picture of a model's scalability with pointwise comparisons at a certain compute-region"); [[moba-mixture-of-block-attention-for]] ("the loss gap is progressively narrowing"; 0.105 -> 0.045 nats across its sweep); [[memory-grafting-scaling-language-model]] (MoE 45.62 / vanilla Engram 45.03 at 0.92B vs 51.95 / 52.43 at 2.8B); [[quantifying-pretraining-variance-data-initialization-and-floating-point-arithmet]] ("Within-group standard deviations are <=0.004 for every category"); [[datadecide-how-to-predict-best-pretraining-data-with-small-experiments]] (2pp run-to-run std at 1B/5xC).
findings.recommendation: Add two sentences and one small table to 'The measurement problem is a unit problem'. First, state the projection: "Both deltas are 100-500B-token measurements; scaled to 9B by ln(tokens) they are ~0.0066 and ~0.029 nats -- 1.7x and 7.2x the 0.004 floor, so the Engram arm is marginal and the OE arm is detectable." Second, state the asymmetry: "A null is a bound; a win is not a verdict either, because the scaling exponent differs by architecture and the dense Transformer's is steepest (alpha 0.54 vs 0.23 Switch, 0.25 Performer), so a 9B ranking flatters every non-dense arm and can reverse at 100B." Then change the Verdict's 'Adequate for the upper half, not for a verdict' to 'Adequate for a bound, not for a ranking', and add the exponent table (dense 0.54/0.28, Switch 0.23/0.14, Performer 0.25/0.05) as the mechanism.

findings.location: ## DDP Overhead Model -> ### The joint re-derivation. Anchor quote: "The net effect is 36% → 6.6%."
findings.issue: The section shows two factors but does not carry the derivation through, and its headline is not reproducible from its own numbers. (a) The units basis flips mid-derivation: 2.7 s is 2.0 GiB / 0.75 GiB/s, while 3.98 s is 2.0 GB / 0.503 GB/s. On a consistent basis the numerator grows 1.60x, not 1.48x; 7.6/1.60 = 4.75, not 5.4; and 36% / 4.75 = 7.7%, not 6.6%. The report's own table row gives 7.1% ("32k, 450 TFLOPS, busbw reading (3.2 GB wire at 0.805 GB/s) | 56.3 s | 4.0 s | 7.1%"), so prose and table disagree -- and 6.6% is then quoted five times downstream (intro, 'derived 6.6%', MoE 47%, Verdict (a), claim table). (b) The 2.0 GB payload silently assumes bf16 gradient buckets. Under standard AMP the parameters and gradients are fp32 (ptrblck: "The parameters are stored in float32 using the automatic mixed-precision util. and thus also the gradients. NCCL thus communicates them in float32, too"), so the payload is 4.0 GB and the overhead doubles to ~14% at the corrected window. The interim note calls bf16_compress_hook "a load-bearing premise of the feasibility claim", not an optional optimisation -- and it carries a precision cost the report never states: NCCL's bf16 ring reduction is its least numerically stable configuration (Jeaugey: "The least stable algorithm is rings"), and on a single-node 5-GPU box the tree degenerates to a chain, so there is no stability escape hatch. (c) The Training Topologies 'corrected comparison' table's two quantitative columns are not commensurable: 'Per-GPU volume' mixes gradient payload (DDP 2.0 GB, ZeRO-2 2.0 GB, FSDP 3.0 GB, PP 134 MB/hand-off) with wire volume (TP 126 GB, which is 1.6x the payload on a five-way ring), and 'Overhead vs 56.3 s' mixes percentages (6.6%, 4-14%) with ratios (2.8x, 1.4x). A reader comparing 2.0 GB to 126 GB concludes TP is 63x worse; the wire comparison is 3.2 vs 126 = 39x, and the overhead column says 2.8x. The table's own claim -- "TP and EP are not expensive so much as unavailable or badly placed" -- is contradicted by TP's 2.8x, which is expensive.
findings.evidence: interim-report-allreduce-ceiling-and-definition, section 'The bf16 sub-question: resolved, and the answer is the opposite of the hypothesis': "its 2.0 GB payload for 1B trainable params is 2 bytes/param, i.e. it already assumes bf16 buckets. Without the hook (fp32 buckets) the payload is 4.0 GB and the overhead doubles to ~108% at 1M tokens under the busbw reading. So the hook is not an optional optimisation to be tested later (repo open question #2); it is a **load-bearing premise of the feasibility claim**. And it carries a precision cost the repo does not budget: bf16 ring accumulation is the least numerically stable configuration NCCL has (Jeaugey: 'The least stable algorithm is rings'), and on a single-node 5-GPU box the tree degenerates to a chain, so there is no stability escape hatch." Same note, section 'The definitional question is settled; the numeric question is not': "busbw = 1.6 x algbw at N=5, by construction ... the repo's 0.805 GB/s is 75-86% of the busbw band (a plausible, slightly conservative measurement) and 1.29-1.48x the algbw band (not plausible)." Primary sources: [[does-nccl-allreduce-use-fp16-mixed-precision-pytorch-forums]] (ptrblck: AMP keeps fp32 params and fp32 gradients); [[reduce_kernelh]] (native __hadd/__hadd2 bf16 under __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 800); [[half-precision-reduction-accumulation-in-fp32-issue-1026-nvidianccl-github]] (Jeaugey on ring instability); [[demystifying-nccl-an-in-depth-analysis-of-gpu]] (tree degenerates to a chain on a single node); [[pytorch-ddp-comm-hooks-default_hookspy-bf16fp16-compress-hooks]] (the hook); [[performancemd-2]] and [[all_reducecu]] (busbw = algbw x 2(n-1)/n).
findings.recommendation: Rewrite 'The joint re-derivation' to carry one basis end to end: payload 2.0 GB bf16, rate 0.805 GB/s busbw -> 0.503 GB/s algbw, comm 3.98 s, compute 56.3 s, overhead 7.1%; show 1.60x, 7.6x and 4.75x; then replace every downstream 6.6% with 7.1% (intro, 'derived 6.6%', MoE 47% -> 50%, Verdict (a), claim table). Add a sentence stating the hook premise: "This payload requires bf16_compress_hook; under standard AMP the buckets are fp32, the payload is 4.0 GB, and the overhead is ~14%. The hook is a load-bearing premise, not an optimisation, and bf16 ring accumulation is NCCL's least stable mode with no tree escape hatch on a single node." Finally, reconcile the Training Topologies table: normalize 'Per-GPU volume' to wire bytes per GPU per step (DDP 3.2 GB, ZeRO-2 3.2 GB, FSDP 4.8 GB, PP 134 MB/hand-off, TP 126 GB, EP 62.9 GB) and express every overhead as a percentage of the 56.3 s window (DDP 7.1%, ZeRO-2 7.1%, FSDP 10.7%, PP 4-14%, TP 280%, EP 140%), with a footnote that EP's 140% is serial and overlaps with expert compute. Also fix the claim table's '1.29-1.48x the algbw band' to '1.20-1.39x' (0.805 GB/s against the 0.58-0.67 GB/s band).

findings.location: ## CSA2 at 32k -> ### The memory objection is soft; the architecture objection is hard. Anchor quote: "it is a kernel-porting project"
findings.issue: The section lists five stacks and quotes FlashMLA's scope, but never gives the mechanism that makes the port hard, so 'kernel-porting project' is asserted rather than argued. Four pieces are missing. (a) wgmma vs mma.sync: TileLang's DSA stack is built on Hopper wgmma.mma_async ("On SM90 the fp8 form of wgmma.mma_async has no imm-trans-a / imm-trans-b operands"), and Ampere has only mma.sync. TileLang can emit mma.sync, so an sm_80 build is not architecturally impossible -- but "Without a K-major V, T.gemm falls back to mma.sync and the whole kernel runs 1.81x slower", and nothing in the stack has been compiled or measured for sm_80. That nuance matters: it tells the reader the port is possible-but-slow rather than impossible, which is a different recommendation. (b) The decisive quantitative fact is absent: StreamIndex's Triton attention forward "at V4-Pro dimensions reaches only 8% of the H200 BF16 peak (versus TileLang's 40% peak with the same shape)", so even a successful Triton port would not produce a usable training kernel -- "At 8% of peak, even a 64x FLOP reduction does not produce a usable training kernel." (c) The report says to write "an sm_80 indexer backward and an sm_80 sparse-MLA backward" but gives no reason to believe the indexer is the hard one. HISA measures on A100: "With 2048 selected tokens, the Sparse MLA operator consistently costs about 1.6 ms, while the indexer reaches 5.6 ms at 64K context length ... the main performance bottleneck in DSA lies in the indexer rather than in Sparse MLA itself." (d) The layer mix is absent: V4.1-Flash ships 2 SWA + 4 Full + 4 Reindex + 30 Reuse over 40 layers, so 32 of 40 (80%) run no indexer at all, and the 16,384-candidate cap binds on only the 4 decoder Reindex layers. The report names the cap in its section intro and never returns to it, so the reader cannot see that the indexer overhead applies to 20% of layers -- and cannot see that attention density at 32k is set by top-k 512 of 32,768 (1.56%, 64x FLOP reduction) whether or not the cap binds.
findings.evidence: interim-report-csa2-at-32k-sm80, section 'The architecture objection is the hard blocker, and it is harder than the locus stated': "The StreamIndex row is the crucial nuance: it does ship a Triton sparse-attention backward (sparse_attn_bwd.py, 'atomic-scatter dKV') and a Triton chunked indexer -- an arch-portable full training stack. But the repo says plainly 'Tested on H100 / H200 (Hopper, sm_90a)', and the paper lists 'multi-hardware validation on H100, A100, and MI300X' as future work. Its own Triton attention forward 'reaches about 8% of H200 BF16 peak at V4-Pro dimensions (d_h = 512)' -- against TileLang's 40% on the same shape. At 8% of peak, even a 64x FLOP reduction does not produce a usable training kernel." Same note, section 2: "The kernels are explicitly built around Hopper primitives ... wgmma is Hopper-only; Ampere has only mma.sync. TileLang can emit mma.sync (the note records a fallback: 'Without a K-major V, T.gemm falls back to mma.sync and the whole kernel runs 1.81x slower'), so an sm_80 build is not architecturally impossible -- but nothing in this stack has been compiled or measured for sm_80, and the tuned schedule is Hopper's." Same note, section 'The repo's reasoning is wrong in a way the locus also gets wrong': "V4.1-Flash's shipped 40-layer mix is 2 SWA + 4 Full + 4 Reindex + 30 Reuse (3 encoder Full + 1 decoder Full; 4 decoder Reindex; 15 encoder + 15 decoder Reuse). That is 32 of 40 layers (80%) running no indexer at all ... the cap binds on exactly the 4 decoder Reindex layers -- 10% of layers." Same note, section 'Position C': "HISA: 'With 2048 selected tokens, the Sparse MLA operator consistently costs about 1.6 ms, while the indexer reaches 5.6 ms at 64K context length. This suggests that the main performance bottleneck in DSA lies in the indexer rather than in Sparse MLA itself.' All comparisons 'conducted on an NVIDIA A100 GPU'." Primary sources: [[tilelangexamplesdeepseek_v32-at-main-tile-aitilelang-github]] (wgmma; 1.81x mma.sync fallback; 25.79 ms vs 14.24 ms at S=8192); [[streamindex-memory-bounded-compressed-sparse]] (8% of H200 peak at d_h=512); [[published-as-a-conference-paper-at-colm-2026]] (HISA 1.6 ms MLA vs 5.6 ms indexer at 64K on A100); [[deepseek-v41-flash]] SS4.2.1 (layer mix); [[longcat-sparse-attention-taming-the-lightning-via]] (4.5% of peak gather; 0.83x at 32K).
findings.recommendation: Add a 'Why the port is hard' paragraph after the five-row stack table. It should say: (1) the tuned stacks are built on Hopper wgmma.mma_async; Ampere has only mma.sync, and TileLang's own fallback runs 1.81x slower, so the port is possible-but-slow rather than impossible; (2) the one arch-portable Triton stack reaches 8% of H200 peak at d_h=512 against TileLang's 40%, so even a successful port would not produce a usable training kernel -- that is the decisive reason not to attempt it; (3) the indexer, not the sparse MLA, is the bottleneck (HISA on A100: 1.6 ms MLA vs 5.6 ms indexer at 64K), so the indexer backward is the hard half; (4) V4.1-Flash runs an indexer on only 8 of 40 layers and the 16,384-candidate cap binds on 4 of them, so the indexer overhead applies to 20% of layers -- which is why the cap is not the lever the repo thinks it is, and why attention density (top-k 512 of 32,768 = 1.56%, 64x) is the right quantity.

findings.location: ## MoE & EP -> ### MoE is the wrong axis for this box. Anchor quote: "so MoE spends the scarce resource to save the abundant one"
findings.issue: The section rests on the availability argument and the 'wrong axis' claim, and both are under-argued. (a) The 'wrong axis' claim needs the trade rate and contradicts the report's own PP=5 finding. MoE does not spend more memory than a dense model of the same total parameters: a 7B-total/1B-active MoE and a 7B dense model both need 33.6 GB/card under ZeRO-2 (168 GB aggregate), but the MoE computes 1B FLOPs/token against the dense model's 7B. The real trade is 7x capacity for 7x memory at 1x FLOPs, and the Training Topologies section already says PP=5 fits that 7B at 25.8 GB/card with 38 GB of headroom and a 4-14% bubble -- "it trains the experts without freezing anything". So the MoE arm is feasible under PP=5, and 'MoE is the wrong axis' is a deprioritisation, not a feasibility verdict. The report never reconciles the two, so the reader cannot tell whether to run the MoE arm. (b) The production literature that would calibrate EP's cost is gone. DeepSeek-V3 measured "an inefficient computation-to-communication ratio of approximately 1:1" for cross-node EP on 2048 H800s with NVLink + InfiniBand -- the single most persuasive number for 'EP is not for this box', because it is what EP costs on the best fabric in existence; the report has DualPipe's 'near-zero all-to-all' but not the 1:1 baseline that motivates DualPipe. DeepSpeed-MoE's production instance of the total/active asymmetry is absent: 1.3B+MoE-128 is 52B total (40x), and it trains at 372 samples/s against 70 for a 6.7B dense model on 128 A100s -- 5x faster at 8x the parameters. Piper's answer to MoE training is absent: "It organizes P GPUs into a PP x EP [grid]", which is exactly the PP=5 route the report recommends elsewhere. (c) The 1.4x EP estimate is serial (78 s / 56.3 s) but the section then says "EP's all-to-all can overlap with expert computation", which would make the cost max(compute, comm), not compute + comm -- the report never says which governs.
findings.evidence: interim-report-topology-cost-at-1m-tokens, section 'Position E: "EP is ruled out by the fabric" -- its best case, and the better reason': "The repo's arithmetic case is directionally right but numerically weak: ~6x compute (per-GPU volume at the wire rate), not 72x. The stronger case is a software barrier ... So EP is ruled out for a reason the repo does not give: no EP library runs on this fabric at all." Same note, section 4: "Their 1.3B+MoE-128 model 'will only activate 1.3B parameter per token' ... but the model 'has roughly 8x the parameters of the corresponding dense model (e.g., 6.7B dense model has 6.7 billion parameters and 1.3B+MoE-128 has 52 billion parameters)'. That is a 40x total/active ratio (52B/1.3B). Training throughput on 128 A100s: 372 samples/s for the 52B-total MoE against 70 samples/s for the 6.7B dense model -- 5x faster at 8x the parameters." Same note, section 6: "Piper closes this gap by composing pipeline parallelism with expert parallelism. It organizes P GPUs into a PP x EP [grid]." Same note, committed position: "PP is the correct training topology for the 7B-total/~1B-active MoE arm at 1M-token global batches on this box -- DDP cannot fit it and FSDP costs 1.5x DDP's bytes for the same total params -- while DDP remains the right default for the <=1.5B-trainable frozen-table arm." Primary sources: [[deepseek-v3-technical-report]] ("the communication overhead introduced by cross-node expert parallelism results in an inefficient computation-to-communication ratio of approximately 1:1"); [[deepspeed-moe-advancing-mixture-of-experts-inference]] (52B/1.3B; 372 vs 70 samples/s on 128 A100s; "5x training cost reduction"); [[piper-efficient-large-scale-moe-training-via]] (PP x EP grid; 2-3.5x MFU over X-MoE); [[scalable-training-of-mixture-of-experts-models-with]] ("MoE training is fundamentally communication-bound unless parallelism is designed specifically for this asymmetry").
findings.recommendation: Restore a production-literature paragraph to 'The bandwidth case evaporates' with the DeepSeek-V3 1:1 ratio, the DeepSpeed-MoE 40x ratio and 372-vs-70 samples/s, and Piper's PP x EP composition -- the last of which is the constructive route the report already recommends. Then rewrite 'MoE is the wrong axis' to give the trade rate and reconcile with PP=5: "MoE buys 7x capacity for 7x memory at 1x FLOPs. Under ZeRO-2 that is 33.6 GB/card -- the same as a dense 7B -- and under PP=5 it is 25.8 GB/card with 38 GB of headroom. So the MoE arm is feasible; it is deprioritised because the 9B budget cannot resolve its effect, not because the box cannot run it." Finally, state whether the 1.4x EP estimate is serial or overlapped, and if overlapped give max(compute, comm) rather than compute + comm.

findings.location: ## Source Tensions. Anchor quote: "Five disputes in the source base bear directly on the argument above."
findings.issue: The section's own promise is not kept, and the single most important tension in the corpus is missing. (a) The 5-GPU ring pathology is absent everywhere in the report. The report's entire communication calibration assumes a clean 2(N-1)/N = 1.6 ring-load factor at N=5, but the only published measurement of 5-GPU PCIe collectives warns against exactly this configuration: "the NUMA effects appear quite significant with 5 GPUs, implying that there may be a congestion when forming a NCCL ring among 5 GPUs. One should avoid adopting 5 GPUs in their application setup" (Li/Song/Barker, PNNL, IEEE TPDS). That pushes the ceiling down and the 6.6%/7.1% up, and it is the one source that directly attacks the report's central number. The report even says "the corpus contains no five-rank all-reduce at any width" -- so it knows the measurement gap -- but never says the one published 5-GPU study warns against 5 GPUs. (b) The host-staged saturation plateau is absent: a Gen3 x16 A6000 box delivers 4.3 GB/s busbw, only 1.01-1.16x the CMP box's Gen2 x16 figure of 3.69-4.24 GB/s, despite roughly double the line rate -- so link generation stops mattering above Gen2 for host-staged collectives, which is what bounds the capacitor mod's payoff and makes Gen3's fuse-block irrelevant in a way the report does not state. (c) One of the five items does not resolve to a number: 'Every sparse-attention 32k win is an adaptation-stage result' sets the plan against the sources rather than two sources against each other, and resolves to 'the plan sits outside the regime' with no number change -- violating the section's stated contract, and duplicating the CSA2 section's 'The regime point is the last piece'.
findings.evidence: interim-report-allreduce-ceiling-and-definition, section 'What the corpus already said': "Two corpus facts sharpen the 5-rank case specifically. [[evaluating-modern-gpu-interconnect-pcie]] (Li/Song/Barker, PNNL, IEEE TPDS) states: 'the NUMA effects appear quite significant with 5 GPUs, implying that there may be a congestion when forming a NCCL ring among 5 GPUs. One should avoid adopting 5 GPUs in their application setup.' And for PCIe, 'CL bandwidth decreases with more GPUs, which is due to bus contention in a tree-network', with all-reduce showing 'the largest latency' of the five collectives. So the N=5 penalty is likely worse than the 1.6x ring-load factor alone -- which pushes the ceiling down, not up." Same note, section 'Does the 24-capacitor x16 mod multiply it?': "the host-staged path saturates: the A6000 box at Gen3 x16 (roughly double Gen2 x16's line rate) delivers 4.3 GB/s busbw, only 1.01-1.16x the CMP box's Gen2 x16 figure. So the mod captures essentially all the available gain and a hypothetical Gen3 unlock would buy ~nothing." Same note, open questions: "No 5-rank measurement exists at any width. Every receipt is 2-4 ranks. The Tartan warning that 5-GPU PCIe rings are pathological means the N=5 penalty may exceed the 1.6x ring-load factor, which would push the ceiling below the values derived here. A 5-rank run at x4 and at x16 is the single highest-value experiment in the program." Primary sources: [[evaluating-modern-gpu-interconnect-pcie]] (5-GPU NUMA warning; PCIe CL bandwidth decreases with GPU count); [[ddp-on-a-pcie-only-4x-rtx-a6000-no-nvlink-plain-ddp-gave-2x-bf16-gradient-compre]] ("NCCL bus bandwidth between the four cards was 4.3 GB/s ... flat from 8 MB to 1 GB messages"); [[readmemd]] (3.69-4.24 GB/s at Gen2 x16).
findings.recommendation: Replace the thin 'Every sparse-attention 32k win is an adaptation-stage result' item (its content already appears in the CSA2 section's 'The regime point is the last piece') with the 5-GPU pathology tension, which does resolve to a number: "The corpus's own bandwidth calibration assumes a clean 1.6 ring-load factor at N=5, but the only published measurement of 5-GPU PCIe collectives says to avoid 5 GPUs because NUMA congestion degrades the ring. The 1.6 factor is therefore a floor, not a ceiling, and the 7.1% carries an unquantified N=5 penalty -- which is why a 5-rank all_reduce_perf is the highest-value measurement in the program." Then add the saturation plateau as a sixth item or fold it into 'Width is not speed': "A Gen3 x16 host-staged box measures 4.3 GB/s busbw, only 1.01-1.16x the CMP box's Gen2 x16 figure -- so the capacitor mod captures essentially all the available gain and Gen3's fuse-block costs nothing."

findings.location: ## Verdict. Anchor quote: "Four measurements would settle the premises, and none is expensive:"
findings.issue: The report gives four premise checks and a lever ranking but no experiment program: no ordering, no wall-clock cost, no decision gates, no statistical design. The query's first clause asks 'which LLM training experiments are feasible', and the report answers with claim verdicts plus premise measurements. The interim token-budget note supplies a concrete affordable design the report never mentions: a 4-size ladder (50M/125M/250M/500M) x 2 architectures = 8 runs, each trained to ~1/3 of budget with the first 10% of checkpoints discarded ("It is generally possible to estimate a model's final loss beginning roughly 1/3 of the way through training"), fitting L(C) per architecture and comparing exponents rather than single losses, at 8K context -- ~12-35 wall-clock days, the same envelope already planned. It also supplies the decoupling the report lacks: "the 32k context requirement should be decoupled from the architecture comparison. The memory and MoE axes do not need 32k ... Running the ladder at 8K instead of 32k cuts FLOPs/token by ~3x". And the 5-arm wall-clock that makes 'match the literature' unaffordable: 100B/arm = 77 days, 5 arms = 386 days. The report's only design statement is "the 9B A/B plus a second seed if the delta lands within 2x of the floor" -- which, per depth-3, is the design the evidence says cannot resolve a ranking. The four measurements are also unsequenced and uncosted: the GQA check is free and gates the sparse arm, but the report lists it fourth, after three hardware measurements.
findings.evidence: interim-report-token-budget-and-effect-size, section 'What the design should be instead, at the same wall-clock': "1. Replace the single-point A/B with a size ladder. [[a-hitchhikers-guide-to-scaling-law-estimation]]: '5 models is a safe bet ... These models can be small' ... A 4-size ladder (50M / 125M / 250M / 500M) x 2 architectures = 8 runs. Fitting L(C) per architecture and comparing exponents is what resolved MoBA's 1e-3-nat gap at 8K -- a gap ~100x below the noise floor that no single-point comparison could have seen. 2. Train each ladder point to ~1/3 of budget, not to completion ... That cuts the ladder's wall-clock by ~3x, which is what makes 8 runs affordable. 3. Pick the metric for spread, not for convention." Same note, section 'The wall-clock ceiling': "at the measured ~15k tok/s, 100B per arm is 77 wall-clock days and five arms is 386 days." Same note, section 'What the design should be instead': "Running the ladder at 8K instead of 32k cuts FLOPs/token by ~3x (T4: 2.554e10 -> 8.64e9 for 500M/28L/2048), which turns a 35-day program into a ~12-day one, or buys 3x more ladder points for the same wall-clock. Only the CSA2 arm needs 32k, and it should get a small budget plus the phase-stratified metric." Primary sources: [[a-hitchhikers-guide-to-scaling-law-estimation]] ("5 models is a safe bet"; "estimate a model's final loss beginning roughly 1/3 of the way through training"; "As long as the first ~10% of checkpoints are discarded"); [[datadecide-how-to-predict-best-pretraining-data-with-small-experiments]] ("The evaluation must separate pairs ... by an amount greater than combined noise"; metric choice moves code-task decision accuracy from trivial to 80%); [[periodic-weak-spots]] ("average accuracy is not enough to evaluate models with chunked KV-cache compression. Their reliability should also be measured across phases"); [[moba-mixture-of-block-attention-for]] (1e-3-nat gap resolved by the scaling-law fit).
findings.recommendation: Add a sequenced program after the four measurements, with costs and gates. Suggested structure: (0) the four premise checks -- lspci -vv, 5-rank all_reduce_perf, 250 W GEMM burn, GQA group-size check -- one day total, and the GQA check is a free gate on the sparse arm; (1) if the GQA group size is 1 at 32k, drop the sparse arm before any kernel work; (2) run the memory/MoE axes at 8K on a 4-size ladder (50M/125M/250M/500M x 2 architectures), each to ~1/3 of budget with the first 10% of checkpoints discarded, fitting L(C) and comparing exponents -- ~12-35 days, and this is the only design in the evidence that resolves deltas below the noise floor; (3) run CSA2/NSA alone at 32k with a small budget and a phase-stratified metric. State the 5-arm wall-clock at 100B/arm (386 days) so the reader can see why 'match the literature' is not an option. Replace 'the 9B A/B plus a second seed' with this program, or state explicitly that the 9B A/B is a bound-generator and not a ranking instrument.
